title: Corneal and subtarsal foreign body removal
subtitle: Slit-lamp removal, rust ring, and ruling out a penetrating injury

sources.title: Clinical Management Guideline: Foreign body, corneal

indications: A superficial corneal or conjunctival foreign body.
A subtarsal foreign body causing linear corneal abrasions.
contraindications: Suspected penetrating injury: high-velocity mechanism (hammering metal on metal, grinding), a positive Seidel test, an irregular pupil, shallow chamber or hyphaema. Shield and refer; do not remove at the slit lamp.
A deep stromal or central foreign body beyond the operator's competence.
preparation: History of the mechanism; visual acuity before anything else.
Fluorescein at the slit lamp, including a Seidel test; evert the upper lid.
Orbit X-ray or CT when a high-velocity metallic fragment is possible (never MRI).
positioning: Seated at the slit lamp, chin on the rest and forehead against the band, eyes looking at a fixation target.
equipment: Slit lamp, topical anaesthetic, fluorescein, sterile cotton buds, 25G or 27G needle (bevel up) or a foreign body spud, a battery-powered burr for rust rings, antibiotic ointment or drops.
anatomy: The corneal epithelium and Bowman's layer superficially; the central visual axis; the upper tarsal conjunctiva where subtarsal foreign bodies lodge.
criticalSafety: Exclude a penetrating injury before removing anything.
Approach the cornea tangentially with the needle bevel up, never towards the eye.
Avoid deep digging in the visual axis.
commonErrors: Missing an intraocular foreign body after a high-velocity injury.
Pointing the needle at the eye.
complications: Missed intraocular foreign body and endophthalmitis or siderosis.
postop: Antibiotic ointment or drops for several days; no patch routinely.
Review if a rust ring was left or the defect was large.
Return the same day for increasing pain, discharge or reduced vision; eye protection at work.

steps.emphasis: Verbal consent; record the visual acuity first.
At the slit lamp, chin on the rest, forehead against the band, fixating on a target.
Antibiotic cover and clear return advice; eye protection advice for work.

step.fb.mechanism-check.title: Mechanism and penetrating injury check
step.fb.mechanism-check.why: A tiny entry wound from a high-velocity metal fragment can hide an intraocular foreign body. Removing what is visible on the surface and sending the patient home misses it.
how: Ask how it happened: hammering metal on metal, grinding, or anything high-velocity raises suspicion of penetration.
Look for a full-thickness wound, a positive Seidel test, an irregular pupil, a shallow chamber, hyphaema or a lens opacity.
If suspected, stop: shield the eye, nil by mouth, imaging (X-ray or CT, never MRI) and urgent ophthalmology.

step.fb.evert.title: Everting the upper lid
step.fb.evert.why: Subtarsal foreign bodies scratch the cornea with every blink and are missed if the lid is not everted.
how: Ask the patient to look down; evert the upper lid over a cotton bud placed at the upper border of the tarsus.
Sweep the tarsal conjunctiva with a moist cotton bud; double-evert with a retractor if the history suggests a particle high in the fornix.
pitfalls: Not everting the lid when there are vertical linear abrasions.

step.fb.remove.title: Removing the foreign body and rust ring
step.fb.remove.why: Removal should take the foreign body and as little cornea as possible. The needle always approaches tangentially, bevel up, so a sudden movement cannot drive it into the eye.
how: Try a moist cotton bud first for loose particles.
For embedded particles, rest your hand on the patient's cheek and lift the particle out with the bevel of a 25G or 27G needle held tangentially to the cornea.
Remove a rust ring with a burr gently; leave a deep or central residue for review in a day or two, when it loosens.
pitfalls: Digging deep in the visual axis.

step.fb.fluorescein.title: Fluorescein and Seidel check after removal
step.fb.fluorescein.why: Checking the defect afterwards shows its size for follow-up and confirms the cornea is not leaking.
how: Stain with fluorescein; measure the epithelial defect.
Repeat the Seidel test over the site.

step.fb.penetrating-bailout.title: Bailout: a leak or signs of penetration
step.fb.penetrating-bailout.why: If the eye is open, every further manipulation can push contents out. Protecting it and transferring it is the treatment.
how: Stop; do not press on the eye or remove a protruding object.
Apply a rigid shield (no pad), give anti-emetic and analgesia, keep nil by mouth.
Arrange imaging and urgent ophthalmology; consider tetanus status and systemic antibiotics per protocol.
pitfalls: Padding an open globe with pressure.
